title: E-Commerce
part: Part B — Cyber Safety and E-Commerce

blocks.html: Twenty years ago, buying a pair of shoes meant visiting a market. Today a family in Darbhanga can order shoes on a phone at night and receive them in two days. This is e- commerce.
Definition: E-commerce (electronic commerce) is the buying and selling of goods and services, and the transfer of money and data, over the internet.

E-business is wider: it means using the internet for all business activities — buying, selling, serving customers, working with suppliers, hiring, accounting and marketing. Every e-commerce activity is e-business, but not every e-business activity is e-commerce.

blocks.html: Parts of an e-commerce system: website or app with a catalogue → shopping cart → checkout → payment gateway → order management → logistics (warehouse and delivery) → customer support and returns.

blocks.html: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 apply to online shopping. E-commerce companies must:

items.html: show the seller's name, address and contact details;
clearly display the total price, delivery charges, return, refund and warranty policies;
show the country of origin of goods;
appoint a grievance officer and acknowledge complaints within 48 hours;
not use fake reviews or misleading advertisements.

blocks.html: Consumers can complain to the company first, then the National Consumer Helpline (1915) or the e-Daakhil portal for consumer courts.

items.html: Buy from well-known websites and apps; check the URL and https.
Read seller ratings, reviews and the return policy.
Be suspicious of prices that are "too good to be true".
Prefer UPI, cards or cash on delivery; never pay by sending money to a person's account on social media.
Never share OTPs for "refunds" — refunds never need your OTP.
Keep invoices and screenshots of orders.

blocks.html: Did you know? GeM (Government e-Marketplace) lets government offices buy everything from pens to vehicles online, with small businesses and self-help groups able to sell directly to the government.

lessons.title: Workshop 7: Compare and plan an online purchase

blocks.html: Aim: To understand e-commerce from the buyer's and seller's side.

items.html: Compare prices. Choose one product (e.g. a scientific calculator). Find its price on three shopping websites and one local shop. Record price, delivery charge, delivery time and return policy in Excel.
Read the fine print. For one website, find and note the seller's name, the grievance officer's details and the country of origin.
Classify. Make a table of 10 online services your family uses and classify each as B2C, C2C, G2C, etc.
Identify the model. For five apps, decide the business model (marketplace, aggregator, subscription, freemium, advertising).
Plan a small online business. In groups, plan how a local artisan (e.g. bamboo crafts, Madhubani art, makhana) could sell online: products, price, platform, payment options, delivery and returns.
E-commerce is buying and selling over the internet; e-business includes all business activities done online.
E-commerce is open 24 × 7, reaches everywhere and costs less, but customers cannot touch goods and face fraud risks.
Types: B2B, B2C, C2C, C2B, D2C, G2C, G2B and B2G; m-commerce uses mobiles.
Business models: inventory, marketplace, aggregator, subscription, freemium, advertising and dropshipping.
An online purchase passes through catalogue, cart, checkout, payment gateway, order management, logistics and returns.
The Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 protect online shoppers; complaints can go to helpline 1915.
